WHITE GIRL WEDS NEGRO
Groom Is an Aged Farmer Residing Near Woodbury, New Jersey
Camden, N. J., Aug. 16.—Burrell Bland, a colored farmer, aged 61 years, was married Tuesday evening to Elizabeth Haines, a comely white woman, 31 years of age. The ceremony was performed by Justice P. T. Colding, colored, at his office in Camden. Bland lives on a small farm near Woodbury, N. J., while the bride has been a resident of this city. Neither has ever entered upon the sea of matrimony before.
burrell-bland-camden-1900-08-15.A2:
Married Negro Hermit.
Camden, N. J., Aug. 15.—This city has had several sensations in marriages lately, but the most astonishing happened this morning, when Burrell Bland, a 71-year-old negro hermit, living on a small farm a few miles from here, was married to Eliza Haines, a pretty Philadelphia white girl only 20 years of age.

The ceremony was performed by Philip Colling, a colored Justice of the peace. The girl first met Bland while tramping across his farm two weeks ago, and since then has visited him nearly every day.

Her people learned of her visits to the old man for the first time yesterday, and were going to send her away to-day, when she stole a march on them, and slipping across the river, met Bland and was warried.

Her parents and friends, as soon as they learned of the girl's act, started on the couple's trail and threatened to lynch the negro if he does not give the girl up.
burrell-bland-camden-1900-08-15.A4:
WEDS A WHITE GIRL.
The Bridegroom Was an Aged Negro Who Loved the Bride When She Was a Child.
"Boss, we wants to be married."

Justice Colding of Camden looked up from his desk and before him was an old negro, bent with age, with hair as white as snow and face as black as charcoal.

By his side was a young white woman, well dressed, not over thirty years of age. She would not be called pretty, but her features were clear cut and refined. Her voice, too, was soft and well modulated as she asked.

"We don't have to have a license, do we?"

Justice Colding is a negro, but, surprised at this unusual match, he asked the woman why she wanted to marry a colored man.

"Because I learned to love him when I was a little girl," she said. "He worked on my father's farm."

The man said his name was Burrell Bland and his intended wife was Elizabeth Haines of Philadelphia. He lived on his own farm, near Woodbury. Neither had ever been married.

Justice Colding performed the ceremony, at the conclusion of which the old negro took her face between his wrinkled hands and said, fervently:

"De Lord bless you, honey."

The woman began to cry and in response to her aged husband's anxious inquiry, said:

"I don't care what they say, I love you, Uncle Rell."

Justice Colding received a fair-sized fee from the groom, who left the office with his face covered with smiles. The bride was softly weeping.—Philadelphia North American.

joseph-bench-baltimore-1900-08-13.A1:
STEVEDORES ON A STRIKE
They Attack Non-Union Men and Cause Trouble.
Baltimore, Aug. 13.—The strike of the 2000 union stevedores is assuming an ugly aspect, in which minor disturbances are of daily occurrence. A big crowd last night attacked a street car at Locust Point, in which were a number of non-union colored men who had taken the strikers' places, and bombarded it with bricks and other missiles. Tonight they attacked a gang of fifteen colored men as the latter emerged from the Baltimore and Ohio docks at Locust Point, following them several blocks and pelting them with stones and bricks. One of the negroes drew a pistol and fired five shots into the crowd of men, women and boys who were following them. Three of the shots took effect, wounding Henry Preser, Joseph Bensch and Arthur Raynler. None of the wounds is serious. The man who did the shooting, together with his companions, fled and has not yet been arrested.

BALTIMORE, Md., Aug. 13.—The strike of the 2,000 union stevedores who went out last week is assuming an ugly aspect and minor disturbances are a daily occurance. A big crowd last night attacked a street car at Locust Point, in which were a number of nonunion colored men, who had taken the strikers' places, and bombarded it with bricks and other missiles until dispersed by the police. To-night they attacked a gang of fifteen colored men as the latter emerged from the Baltimore & Ohio docks at Locust Point, following them several blocks and pelting them with stones and bricks. One of the negroes drew a pistol and fired five shots into the crowd of men, women and boys who were following them. Three of the shots took effect, wounding Hy Presser, Joseph Bensch and Arthur Raynier. None of the wounds are serious and the man who did the shooting, together with his companions, fled and have not yet been arrested.

MILITIA FOR A HANGING.
Request for Soldiers to Preserve Order at Belair, Md.
der at Belair, Md.

BALTIMORE, Aug. 24.—Judge James D. Watters, of Belair, called on Governor Smith at his city office yesterday, and on behalf of the sheriff and State's Attorney of Harford county requested that a detachment of militia be sent to Belair on Friday, August 31, to guard against any trouble at the hanging of William Black. Judge Watters said that while the execution might pass off quietly it was desired to prevent any possibility of a lynching.

Black, who will undergo the death penalty for a felonious assault on Miss Jessie Bradford on February 21 last, is now in the Baltimore city jail, and the plan is to take him to Belair on the morning of the day of execution.

Governor Smith told Judge Watters that whatever protection was necessary would be given, and it is likely that a company of the Fourth or Fifth Regiment may be called upon for this service.

PLEA FOR BLACK'S LIFE.
Condemned Man's Wife Seeks Governor Smith to Ask Clemency.
Condemned Man's Wife Seeks Governor Smith to Ask Clemency.

ANNAPOLIS, Md., Aug. 28.—The wife of William Black, the colored man sentenced to be hanged on Friday for assaulting Miss Jessie Bradford, near Aberdeen, Harford county, visited the office of Governor Smith yesterday for the purpose of making a plea for clemency.

The Governor is still in Snow Hill and will not return to the city until this afternoon, and Black's wife was obliged to depart without seeing him or being able to present her petition. Governor Smith is considering the advisability of sending a company from the Fifth Regiment and one from the Fourth Regiment to attend the hanging and preserve order.

Sheriff Kinhart, of Harford county, who will hang Black at Belair, was in Baltimore yesterday, and invited Deputy Sheriff Joseph H. Heine to assist him with the execution. Mr. Heine has participated in so many hangings that he has gained the reputation of being an expert and his services are in demand upon such occasions. He will probably go to Belair if agreeable to Sheriff Schwatka.

Sheriff Kinhart said the new scaffold would be completed today. It is similar to the one upon which Amos B. Smith, colored, was hanged at the city jail August 3, only smaller. The trap will be dropped by pulling a lever attached to the side of the steps.

"Like Sheriff Schwatka, I don't want any concealment about it, and want the people to see who pulls the lever," said Sheriff Kinhart. "When I went to see Black Saturday he asked for some whisky and I got him a quart. I will give him everything he wants, and if the county won't pay for it I guess I'll have to. He seems to be breaking down, and I am afraid that we will have trouble with him." The sheriff expects to take Black to Belair Thursday night or Friday morning.

EXECUTION OF WILLIAM BLACK.
Condemned Man to Die for His Crime Tomorrow Morning.
Special Dispatch to The Evening Star.
BELAIR, Harford County, Md., August 30.—Sheriff Andrew Kinhart has everything in readiness for the execution of William Black, colored, who is to die on the scaffold here tomorrow morning for having committed a criminal assault on Miss Jessie Bradford at Aberdeen in March last. The crime was a shocking one, and so aroused the people living about Aberdeen that the prisoner was taken to Baltimore for safe keeping. Sheriff Kinhart has gone to Baltimore for the condemned man and will probably reach here late tonight or at an early hour tomorrow morning, in order that his presence here will not excite the people to violence.

The offer to loan the Baltimore scaffold for the execution was refused, and a new structure has been erected. The scaffold and ropes have been tested and the sheriff anticipates no hitch in tomorrow's proceedings. Black has now made a statement denying the truth of the confession he made shortly after his arrest, but everybody in this vicinity believes the original confession contained the truth. It is believed that he made the denial believing it might change the feeling against him, and insure him a safe transit to the scaffold. The denial, however, has had the opposite effect, and the people are as much, if not more, incensed against him than ever.

Citizens of the county are greatly surprised at the action of Governor Smith, on the request of Judge James D. Watters of the circuit court of Harford county, in sending a company of the state militia here. If the present program is carried out the county seat will be the scene tomorrow of the novel spectacle of troops accompanying a condemned man to the scaffold. The governor decided to send Company G of the 4th Regiment, sixty strong, with the condemned man. This action was taken because it was feared that Black would not be permitted to die on the scaffold if he returned here, with only the sheriff and a few deputies to defend him.

WILLIAM BLACK HANGED.
Negro Who Assaulted Jessie Bradford Near Aberdeen, Md.
BELAIR, Md., August 31. — William Black, colored, was hanged here at 7:41 o'clock this morning. He met death calmly, although he was plainly nervous on his way to the scaffold, and has for several days past been in a state bordering on complete collapse.

Black died for a criminal assault committed on Miss Jessie Bradford, a fifteen-year-old girl, who lived near Aberdeen, this county. The negro overpowered her in a patch of woods on February 21, and was seen struggling with her by the crew of a fast freight train which passed the scene at that time. A searching party was organized, and there is no doubt the negro would have been lynched if caught then, but he made his way to Baltimore, shipped on an oyster boat and was caught down the bay a few days later. His trial and conviction followed, and he has been confined in the Baltimore city jail since then.

Meanwhile another negro, Louis Miller, was lynched in Belair for a similar crime, and threats were made that Black should never die a legal death. For this reason the sheriff of Harford county took unusual precautions, and a company of militia was detailed to attend the execution and preserve order. As a further precaution the announcement was made in the newspapers that the condemned man would be taken to Belair on a morning train and hanged soon after 10 o'clock a.m. Instead of carrying out this program the sheriff put him on a train which reached here from Baltimore shortly after midnight last night, and hanged him this morning before most of the people of Belair were out of their beds.
